items.prompt: Which language is Apple's modern primary language for building native iOS apps?

options.label: Java
Swift
Dart
Kotlin

rubric: Swift is Apple's main language for iOS development.
Kotlin is for Android, Dart is used by Flutter, and Java is mainly Android.

items.prompt: What is the name of the file in an Android app that declares its components and requested permissions?

options.label: AndroidManifest.xml
Info.plist
build.gradle
strings.xml

rubric: AndroidManifest.xml declares components and permissions.
Info.plist is the iOS equivalent; build.gradle configures the build; strings.xml holds text.

items.prompt: Which framework is used to build cross-platform apps with Dart?

options.label: SwiftUI
React Native
Xamarin
Flutter

rubric: Flutter uses Dart.
React Native uses JavaScript, Xamarin uses C#, SwiftUI uses Swift.

items.prompt: What is the term for a single screen of user interface in an Android app, as a basic component?

options.label: Content provider
Activity
Service
Broadcast receiver

rubric: An Activity represents a single screen with a UI.
Service runs background work without UI; the others share data or react to events.

items.prompt: Which store is the official place to distribute iOS apps to the public?

options.label: Microsoft Store
Amazon Appstore
Apple App Store
Google Play Store

rubric: iOS apps are distributed via the Apple App Store.
Google Play is for Android.

items.prompt: Which of the following are device features that an app typically needs the user's permission to access? Select all that apply.

options.label: Reading the device's screen size to lay out its own screens
Camera
Contacts
Storing its own settings in app-private storage

items.prompt: A new developer wants to store a small piece of data, such as a user's chosen theme, on the phone so it remains after the app closes. They ask what simple built-in mechanism is meant for small key-value settings. Which should they name?

options.label: A remote REST endpoint polled at launch
SharedPreferences or UserDefaults
An in-memory variable held in the main screen
A bundled image asset in the app package

rubric: SharedPreferences (Android) and UserDefaults (iOS) store small key-value settings.
An in-memory variable is lost when the app closes.

items.prompt: Why do mobile apps usually ask for permissions at runtime, when a feature is needed, instead of only at install?

options.label: It gives users control and context over sensitive data access
It lets the app skip the operating system's security checks once granted
It removes the need to declare permissions in the app's manifest file
It makes the app download faster because fewer files are bundled in it

rubric: Runtime prompts give users informed control over sensitive access.
Permissions still must be declared; this does not speed downloads or bypass security.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a navigation stack in a mobile app?

options.label: To shrink images so each screen loads faster
To track screens so Back returns to the last one
To queue server requests so they send in order
To save user data on the device between launches

rubric: A stack pushes screens on open and pops them on Back.
It is not for data storage, image handling or networking.

items.prompt: Why should an app fetch data from a remote API off the main (UI) thread?

options.label: Remote servers only accept requests from background threads
Waiting on the network there would freeze the interface
The main thread cannot parse JSON data from a response
Background threads make requests use less mobile data

rubric: Blocking the UI thread makes the app unresponsive.
Servers don't care about threads; JSON parsing and data use are unrelated.

items.prompt: What does it mean that an app moves to the background when the user presses the Home button?

options.label: It is deleted from the device storage
It keeps running at full speed with full access to the screen
It is no longer visible and the system may pause or end it
It is uninstalled and must be re-downloaded

rubric: Backgrounded apps are not visible and can be suspended or killed to free resources.
They are not deleted or uninstalled, and don't keep full priority.

items.prompt: Which describes the difference between a native app and a cross-platform app?

options.label: Native apps cannot use device features like the camera; cross-platform apps can use them
Native apps run only inside a browser; cross-platform apps are installed from a store
Native apps are written once for all platforms; cross-platform apps need separate code
Native uses a platform's own tools; cross-platform shares one codebase across platforms

rubric: Native targets one platform's SDK; cross-platform shares code across iOS and Android.
The other options misstate how each approach works.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain why an app might store data locally on the device? Select all that apply.

options.label: It can make screens load faster
It keeps data available between launches
It removes any need for a server in every app
It lets the app work offline

rubric: Local storage supports offline use, speed and persistence.
It does not eliminate servers for apps that sync or share data.

items.prompt: A learner builds a weather app. When the phone is rotated, the screen layout looks cramped because it was designed for portrait only. A mentor explains the reason for using responsive layouts. What is the best explanation?

options.label: Devices vary in size and orientation, so layouts must adapt
Rotation reloads the screen, so layouts must be rebuilt by hand
Rotation clears the app's stored data, so layouts must reload it
Stores reject portrait-only apps, so layouts must support both

rubric: Screen sizes and orientations vary, so layouts should adapt.
Rotation doesn't erase data and layouts are unrelated to the camera or approval alone.

items.prompt: What happens by default to an Android Activity when the user rotates the device?

options.label: It is moved to a background service and kept alive
It is paused, then resumed with all its state intact
It stays alive and only its layout is stretched to fit
It is destroyed and recreated, losing unsaved state

rubric: By default a configuration change recreates the Activity, so state must be saved or held elsewhere.
Distractors assume the framework preserves state automatically.

items.prompt: In a stack-based navigation model, what does pressing the system Back button do?

options.label: Closes the app and discards every screen stored
Reloads the current screen from the start
Removes the top screen and reveals the one under it
Jumps to the first screen and clears the stack

rubric: Back pops the top screen off the stack and shows the previous one.
Distractors confuse back with reload, reset or exit.

items.prompt: Why must an app ask for camera access at runtime on modern iOS and Android?

options.label: Because camera code cannot compile unless a permission dialog is declared in the source
Because the device only grants camera access to apps bought through the paid store tier
Because the store charges the developer a fee for each permission an app requests
Because the user decides about sensitive access and may revoke it

rubric: Runtime permissions give users control over sensitive device features.
Distractors invent technical or commercial reasons.

items.prompt: Why should network requests not run on the main (UI) thread?

options.label: A slow call would block the UI and freeze the screen
Responses are returned in a format the UI cannot read
Mobile networks only work in background threads
Servers reject requests that come from the UI thread

rubric: The UI thread draws the screen and handles touches, so blocking it freezes the app.
Distractors give false technical limits on networking.

items.prompt: Which kind of data belongs in the platform secure store (Keychain or Keystore) rather than plain preferences?

options.label: The user's chosen app theme
The number of times the app launched
The last screen that was opened
The user's authentication token

rubric: Credentials and tokens are sensitive and need encrypted storage.
Other options are harmless settings that plain preferences handle.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe cross-platform frameworks such as React Native or Flutter? Select all that apply.

options.label: Apps still need platform builds to be submitted to each store
Apps always match fully native performance in every case
Apps skip store review because they run in a shared runtime
One codebase can share most logic between iOS and Android

rubric: Shared code and per-platform builds with store submission are both true.
Distractors overstate performance parity and claim store review is avoided.

items.prompt: A news app fetches articles from an API each time a screen opens and displays them. A user opens the app on a train with no signal and sees a blank screen. Which explanation best fits this behaviour?

options.label: The list component can only render items that were fetched in the last few minutes
The API changed its JSON format during the journey, so parsing fails
The app keeps no local copy, so it has nothing to show offline
The operating system blocks apps from saving data while the device is offline

rubric: Without local caching, the screen depends entirely on the network.
Distractors blame format, rendering or storage limits that don't cause this.

items.prompt: A navigation stack starts empty. The app does: push A, push B, push C, pop, push D, pop. Which screen is on top now?

options.label: B
C
D
A

rubric: Stack goes A,B,C then A,B then A,B,D then A,B, so B is on top.
Distractors come from miscounting the pops.

items.prompt: You declared the camera permission in the manifest or Info.plist. What should the app do next, before opening the camera on a user's tap?

options.label: Store a granted flag in local settings after install, then open the camera directly
Check the permission status and request it if not granted
Open the camera and rely on the declaration to have granted access
Ask for the permission once at first launch and assume it stays granted

rubric: Declaring is not granting; the app must check and request at runtime and handle denial.
Distractors assume the declaration or a stored flag grants access.

items.prompt: A React Native app receives `data = {"user":{"name":"Ana","id":7}}` from the API. Which expression gives the user's name?

options.label: `data.user.name`
`data["Ana"]`
`data.name.user`
`data.user[1]`

rubric: Access nested JSON by following keys: data, user, name.
Distractors reverse keys, use a value as key or use an index.

items.prompt: In a React Native component with `const [count, setCount] = useState(0)`, which handler makes the displayed count increase on a button press?

options.label: `count = count + 1`
`count++` inside the render
`useState(count + 1)`
`setCount(count + 1)`

rubric: The state setter triggers a re-render with the new value.
Distractors change the variable directly or misuse the hook.

items.prompt: You upload an Android update to Google Play and it is rejected because version code 7 was already used. What do you change before rebuilding?

options.label: Uninstall the earlier release from your test device and upload again
Change the app's display name so the store sees a new listing
Switch the build from release to debug mode and upload that
Raise the version code to 8 and rebuild the signed bundle

rubric: Each upload needs a higher version code than any earlier one.
Distractors change unrelated settings; debug builds can't be published.

items.prompt: An API returns 10,000 products. Which choices correctly handle showing them in a list screen? Select all that apply.

options.label: Render all rows at once inside a plain ScrollView
Use a virtualised list such as FlatList or ListView.builder
Refetch the whole list on every key typed in search
Request pages of results as the user scrolls

rubric: Pagination and virtualised lists keep memory and network use low.
Distractors load or fetch everything, which is slow and wasteful.

items.prompt: Your app stores a login token. A request to the API returns 401 Unauthorized because the token expired. The user is on the Orders screen. What should the app do?

options.label: Resend the same request with the same token each second
Keep the token and ask the user to restart the app
Show a blank Orders screen and retry forever
Clear the stored token and navigate to the login screen

rubric: An expired token is invalid, so clear it and send the user to log in again.
Distractors keep using the bad token or leave the user stuck.

items.prompt: An Android screen keeps a `count` in a field of its Activity. After the user rotates the device, `count` resets to 0. Which change keeps the value with the least extra code?

options.label: Lock the orientation to portrait for every user of the app
Hold `count` in a screen-scoped ViewModel and read it from there
Reassign `count` inside `onResume` so it is set after rotation
Call `finish()` before rotation so the screen rebuilds cleanly

rubric: A ViewModel survives configuration changes, so the state persists across rotation.
Locking orientation or reassigning in lifecycle callbacks hides or repeats the reset instead of preserving state.

items.prompt: A photo app needs the user's location only for an optional 'Tag location' button. Where should the runtime location permission request be placed?

options.label: In the manifest declaration alone, because the system grants dangerous permissions at install time
Each time the app returns to the foreground, so the user's consent stays current
Right before the first read of location, triggered by the user choosing that feature
At first launch, before the first screen appears, so the decision is settled early

rubric: Requesting in context, at the moment of use, is the standard flow and gives the user a clear reason.
Upfront or repeated prompts and manifest-only declarations ignore how runtime permissions work.

items.prompt: Your app receives an auth token after login and must keep it on the device between launches. Which storage should you use?

options.label: The platform secure store, such as Keychain or Keystore-backed storage
A text file on shared external storage, so backups can restore it
Plain SharedPreferences or UserDefaults, because reads are fastest there
A constant compiled into the app bundle, so every install has it ready

rubric: Secure stores protect credentials with OS-level encryption and hardware backing.
Plain preferences, bundled constants and shared files can all be read by other parties.

items.prompt: After a successful login, the app opens the Home screen. Pressing Back on Home must not return to the Login screen. What should the navigation code do?

options.label: Restart the app process so the system clears the history
Push Home on top of Login so the user can return to it easily
Hide the Login views but keep Login as the top destination
Navigate to Home and pop Login off the back stack

rubric: Popping Login while navigating removes it from the back stack, so Back leaves the app instead.
Pushing, hiding or restarting leaves Login reachable or is needlessly heavy.

items.prompt: A product list screen opens a detail screen for a product that has 20 fields and several images. Which hand-off is most robust?

options.label: Pass the product ID and let the detail screen load it from the repository
Store the product in a global mutable variable the detail screen reads
Pass the row's list index and look it up in the list's current order
Serialise the whole product object into the navigation arguments

rubric: Passing an ID keeps arguments small and lets the detail screen get fresh data, even after process death.
Large arguments, globals and list indexes are fragile or can point at the wrong item.

items.prompt: You are about to upload a new release build of an Android app to Google Play. Which steps are required? Select all that apply.

options.label: Delete all log statements from your source history
Increase the version code above the previous upload
Mark the app debuggable so crash reports are readable
Sign the bundle with your release or upload key
Build the release variant, not the debug variant

rubric: Release builds, a higher version code and a proper signature are needed for the store to accept the upload.
Debuggable builds are rejected and source history cleanup has no bearing on the upload.

items.prompt: A React Native screen shows 5,000 chat messages by mapping the array into views inside a `ScrollView`. It takes seconds to open and uses a lot of memory. You want a change that keeps all messages scrollable. What should you do?

options.label: Load every message image at full resolution first so scrolling is smooth
Nest the `ScrollView` in another one with a fixed height to cap rendering
Set row opacity to 0 for off-screen messages so they are not drawn
Render the messages with a `FlatList` that only mounts rows near the viewport

rubric: FlatList virtualises rows, creating only those near the viewport, which cuts load time and memory.
Nesting scroll views or hiding rows with opacity still mounts every row.

items.prompt: Push notifications arrive on devices running Android 12 but never appear on devices running Android 13 or later. The server logs show successful delivery to all tokens. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Android 13 removed notification channels, so channel setup throws an error
Battery limits on any device above Android 12 stop every notification
The server rejects tokens from newer devices because their length differs
Newer Android needs a runtime notification permission the app never requests

rubric: Android 13 introduced a runtime notification permission; without a grant, delivered messages are not shown.
The other options contradict the evidence of successful delivery or misdescribe platform changes.

items.prompt: Memory use grows each time the user rotates the device. A heap dump shows dozens of destroyed Activity instances, each referenced by the listener list of a singleton `LocationTracker`. What is the root cause?

options.label: Rotation creates new Activities, and the system never frees old ones itself
The listener list is too large, so it should be replaced with an array
The singleton keeps strong references to listeners that are never unregistered
The Activities declare too many views, which prevents them from being freed

rubric: A long-lived singleton holding strong references to Activities prevents garbage collection, so listeners must be removed on teardown.
The system does free unreferenced Activities, and view count or collection type is not what retains them.

items.prompt: A user edits an item on a detail screen and goes Back, but the list screen still shows the old value until the app restarts. The list loads data once with a one-shot fetch in `onCreate`. Which diagnosis fits?

options.label: The detail screen should have passed the edited value back as a string
The database write failed silently, so the edit was never persisted
The back stack discards the list screen's views and so its data too
The list does not observe the data source, so it never learns of the change

rubric: A one-shot read cannot react to later writes; observing a stream or re-querying fixes it.
Restart showing the new value implies the write succeeded, ruling out the first option.

items.prompt: Profiling shows dropped frames only while scrolling a feed. In each row's bind step the code decodes a 4000-pixel-wide JPEG from disk on the main thread. What is the main cause of the jank?

options.label: The feed holds too many rows in memory, so garbage collection never ends
Deeply nested row layouts make measuring slower than decoding images
Network latency from the API stalls drawing of every visible row
Large bitmap decoding runs on the UI thread and blocks frame rendering

rubric: Decoding big images during bind on the UI thread blocks the frame deadline; decode off-thread at display size.
The profile points to decoding, not network latency, row count or layout depth.

items.prompt: Two phones edit the same note offline. Sync keeps whichever copy has the later device timestamp. Users report a recent edit sometimes disappears after sync. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The local database lacks a primary key, so notes are inserted twice
A device with a clock set ahead stamps older edits as newer and overwrites
REST PUT requests are not idempotent, so retries merge edits wrongly
The server compresses payloads, which drops the final characters of notes

rubric: Last-write-wins on client clocks is vulnerable to clock skew, so an old edit can beat a newer one.
The other causes would produce truncation or duplicates, not lost newer edits.

items.prompt: A feature works in debug builds but crashes at launch in the release build of an Android app. Which are plausible causes? Select all that apply.

options.label: Code shrinking removed model classes that JSON parsing reaches by reflection
Debug builds run on a different programming language than release builds
Release builds disable all network access unless a flag is set
The release signing key's fingerprint is not registered with the sign-in provider

rubric: Shrinking can strip reflectively used classes, and a different signing key can break services that check the fingerprint.
Release builds do not block networking by default and use the same language as debug.

items.prompt: After a token expires, your app fires four API calls at once. Each gets a 401 and each calls the refresh endpoint. The server rotates refresh tokens, invalidating each after one use. Users are randomly logged out. What explains this?

options.label: A CDN caches the refresh endpoint response, so some callers receive stale tokens
The HTTP client does not retry a failed call, so one 401 logs the user out
The access token lifetime is too short, so refresh calls arrive too often for the server
Parallel refreshes send the same refresh token, so later ones fail and force logout

rubric: With rotation, only the first concurrent refresh succeeds; the others use an invalidated token and fail, so refresh should be serialised.
Token lifetime, caching and retries do not explain failures that depend on concurrency.

items.prompt: An Android screen keeps its loaded list and the user's search text in Activity fields. After the device rotates, the list reloads from the network with a flashing spinner and the search text is gone. What is the root cause?

options.label: The list adapter is too large to survive rotation, so the framework discards it and the screen must rebuild it
The Activity is recreated on a configuration change, and the state lived in the instance instead of a ViewModel or saved state
Rotation triggers a low-memory callback, which clears every field of the foreground Activity to recover resources
The network library keeps no cache, so every rotation forces a new request no matter where the screen state is held

rubric: Rotation recreates the Activity, so fields on it are lost unless state is held in a ViewModel or saved state.
Distractors blame caching, memory callbacks or adapter size, which do not explain the lost search text.

items.prompt: A list screen drops frames only when scrolling quickly through rows that show remote photos. Profiling shows long frames on the main thread inside the row-binding code, which decodes each bitmap from raw bytes. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The data set has too many rows for the device, so it must be paginated to twenty items before the frame drops will stop
Decoding runs on the UI thread during binding, so each row blocks rendering; decoding should move off-thread and be cached
The network is too slow, so the list waits for every download to finish before it is able to draw any row on screen
The GPU cannot draw photographic content, so images need converting to vector graphics before they are bound to rows

rubric: Heavy decoding in the bind step blocks the main thread and causes long frames.
Distractors blame row count, network or GPU limits, which the profiler evidence does not support.

items.prompt: An Android app parses API JSON correctly in debug builds. In the release build, with identical code, every parsed model has null fields. The reflection-based JSON library maps keys to field names. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Release builds disable the main thread, so parsed values are never delivered back to the UI layer for display
The store signing process re-encodes response bodies, so JSON keys arrive with different casing than in debug builds
Code shrinking and obfuscation renamed the model fields that reflection matches by name, so JSON keys no longer map
Release builds use HTTP rather than HTTPS, so the server sends a different JSON schema to clients it cannot verify

rubric: Obfuscation renames fields, breaking name-based reflection mapping unless keep rules exist.
Distractors invent transport or signing effects that do not alter response bodies.

items.prompt: A client retries `POST /orders` after a timeout on a flaky connection. Support sees duplicate orders even though users tapped Buy once. Which diagnosis is the most precise?

options.label: The order table lacks an index, so inserts are executed twice whenever the database is under heavy concurrent load
The button handler fires twice because touch events are delivered in pairs on most phones, creating two orders each tap
The retry library caches each response body and replays the stored order to the server every time the app launches
The first attempt succeeded on the server but its response was lost, and the non-idempotent retry created a second order

rubric: A lost response plus a retry of a non-idempotent POST creates duplicates; an idempotency key fixes it.
Distractors invent touch, indexing or caching causes unrelated to retry semantics.

items.prompt: In a tab-based app, tapping the Home tab several times and then pressing Back steps through many copies of Home before the app exits. What best explains this?

options.label: Back navigation on mobile is always linear, so the OS records every tap and replays each one in order on Back
The tab bar caches screenshots of Home, and Back pops each cached image before it shows the real screen
Each tab tap navigates to a new Home instance without single-top or per-tab stack handling, so entries pile up
The Home screen leaks memory, and the leaked copies are what the back button reveals on each successive press

rubric: Navigating without single-top or saved tab stacks pushes duplicate destinations onto the back stack.
Distractors misattribute the behaviour to OS recording, leaks or screenshot caches.

items.prompt: Which of these are likely to leak a destroyed screen (an Activity or view controller) in a mobile app? Select all that apply.

options.label: A ViewModel with a field that holds the Activity it was first created from
A singleton that holds only the application-level context for its work
A singleton that stores the Activity as a callback target and never clears it
A screen that registers a lifecycle-aware observer, which the framework removes when the screen is destroyed

items.prompt: An app sends five parallel requests when a screen opens. The access token has expired, so all five get 401. Each failure handler calls the refresh endpoint, and the server rotates refresh tokens, invalidating the old one on use. Users are randomly logged out. What is the underlying cause?

options.label: The access token lifetime is too short, so lengthening it would remove the 401 responses and the logouts completely
The server rejects parallel requests from one device, so the app must serialize every call through the network layer
The refresh endpoint needs the expired access token in its header, so every refresh attempt fails the same way
Five refreshes race on one refresh token; the first rotates it and the others fail as invalid, which triggers logout

rubric: Concurrent refreshes with a rotating refresh token invalidate each other; a single-flight refresh fixes it.
Distractors treat symptoms or invent server rules that do not match the random pattern.

items.prompt: Six web developers must ship iOS and Android apps in four months. The app is mostly forms, lists and maps with standard UI, plus one camera preview screen with simple overlays. Criteria: time to market, team skills, acceptable native feel. Which approach is best?

options.label: A native iOS app first and Android later, since the team can learn Swift quickly while the first release ships
Two separate native apps, because separate codebases always deliver better performance regardless of what the screens need
A cross-platform framework using a maintained camera plugin, since standard screens dominate and the one special need is covered
A mobile web page saved as a home-screen shortcut, since it avoids the stores and gives full camera overlay control

rubric: A cross-platform framework fits the team's skills and schedule, and the single camera need is met by a plugin.
Distractors ignore the schedule, the team or the platform coverage requirement.

items.prompt: A banking-style app must store an auth token so it survives restarts, resists extraction from backups or rooted devices, and needs no user prompt on each launch. Which storage best meets these criteria?

options.label: Hardware-backed secure storage such as Keychain or a Keystore-encrypted store, which protects the token at rest silently
An obfuscated string constant compiled into the code, since it avoids any storage reads and cannot change at runtime
Plain key-value preferences, since the OS sandbox already guarantees that no other process can ever read the stored file
A local SQLite column holding a Base64 value, since encoding makes the token unreadable inside device backups

rubric: Keychain or Keystore-backed storage gives protection at rest, persistence and no extra prompts.
Distractors rely on sandbox trust, obfuscation or encoding, none of which is real protection.

items.prompt: A release includes a local database schema migration, and installed builds cannot be recalled. Criteria: limit how many users a failure reaches, detect crashes early, and keep the option to halt. Which release approach is best?

options.label: Release to a week-long beta list and then ship to all users, since beta testers usually cover the device and data states of the install base
A staged rollout to a small percentage with crash monitoring, halting expansion if migration failures appear
Release to everyone on a weekend, when lower traffic means fewer people are exposed to any migration bug that appears
Release to all users at once, because the migration passed on the QA team's own test devices and a hotfix can follow if needed

rubric: A staged rollout with monitoring limits exposure and allows halting before wider impact.
Distractors either expose everyone or assume test and beta groups represent every device and data state.

items.prompt: A chat app must show messages within seconds while open, keep battery drain low, and deliver alerts when the app is closed. Which update strategy best fits these criteria?

options.label: Poll every fifteen minutes in a background task, which saves the most battery and is acceptable for chat users
Poll the server every few seconds in all app states, which is simple to build and keeps latency low everywhere
Hold a socket open while foregrounded and use push when backgrounded, balancing latency and battery
Rely on push notifications alone and skip fetching while the app is open, since push carries the full message to the device

rubric: A foreground socket plus background push meets latency, battery and closed-app delivery needs.
Distractors drop one criterion: battery, foreground latency or reliable delivery.

items.prompt: A photo app needs camera access, and on iOS a denied system prompt cannot be shown again by the app. Criteria: maximise the grant rate and avoid wasting the one prompt. When should the app ask?

options.label: At first launch before any screen appears, so the decision is out of the way early and is never repeated
When the user taps capture, after a short in-app explanation, so the system prompt arrives with clear context
After the first denial, since a second prompt can show more users an explanation of why the app needs it
For every permission the app might ever use at first launch, so later features never need another prompt

rubric: Asking in context after a brief rationale improves grants and protects the one-shot prompt.
Distractors ask without context or assume a re-prompt exists, which wastes or misunderstands the single chance.

items.prompt: A backend must make a breaking change to a response format, but old app versions cannot be force-updated for weeks. Which approaches are sound given that constraint? Select all that apply.

options.label: Return a minimum supported version signal so apps can prompt for update before old endpoints are retired
Keep serving the old format on the existing versioned endpoint until adoption of the new app passes a set threshold
Rename fields in place, since installed apps will ignore unknown names and keep working exactly as before
Gate the new behaviour behind server-side feature flags so it can be switched off if the rollout shows errors

rubric: Versioned endpoints, update signals and flags protect old clients during transition.
Renaming fields in place breaks clients that expect the old names, so it fails the stated constraint.

items.prompt: A news feed app is used on poor connections. Product accepts content up to 10 minutes stale but wants the feed to open instantly with no blank screens. Which data approach best meets these criteria?

options.label: Cache raw HTTP responses on disk with a long expiry and refresh them on a daily schedule, since offline use matters more than the ten-minute limit
Keep the last response in an in-memory cache and reuse it on open, since memory reads are the fastest option available on both platforms
Fetch from the network on each open and show a loading spinner until it returns, since fresh data avoids staleness complaints
Render from a local database first, refresh in the background, and update the UI from database changes

rubric: A local database as the source of truth with background refresh gives instant open and bounded staleness.
Distractors either block on the network, lose data on process death or ignore the staleness limit.

items.prompt: A notes app syncs between a phone and a tablet, and both work offline. Criteria: no silent loss of edits, no reliance on device clocks, minimal user interruption. Which conflict strategy is best?

options.label: Keep the copy with more content, because the longer version is likelier to hold the user's latest work
Last-write-wins using each device's local timestamp, because it is simple and needs no extra server logic or user prompts
Take a server-side lock when a note is opened, so two devices can never edit it concurrently, even while offline
Merge per field using server-issued version numbers, and prompt only when both sides edited the same field

rubric: Per-field merge with server versions avoids clock skew and silent loss, and interrupts only on true conflicts.
Local-timestamp last-write-wins loses edits and trusts skewed clocks; a lock cannot be taken offline.

items.prompt: A chat app must show new messages within seconds while backgrounded, on iOS and Android, with minimal battery drain. Which approach is the best fit?

options.label: Run a background loop or foreground service that polls the server every 15 seconds to keep latency low
Send a silent push as a ping, then load the message content when the user next opens the app to save battery
Hold a persistent background WebSocket on both platforms so messages arrive directly without relying on push services
Use a high-priority APNs/FCM push to wake the app, then fetch the message content over the network

rubric: Platform push wakes the app cheaply and the content is then fetched, meeting latency and battery criteria.
Background sockets and polling are throttled or killed by the OS and drain battery.

items.prompt: A banking app pins the server's leaf certificate. Certificates rotate every 90 days and old app versions stay installed for months. Which critique is most valid?

options.label: Pinning must be removed, because app stores reject apps that perform their own trust evaluation of server certificates
Pinning adds no protection beyond TLS, because any trusted CA can already issue a valid certificate for the domain
Leaf pinning is fine, but rotation should be shortened to 30 days so a stolen key stays useful for less time
With no backup pin, a routine rotation locks out installed versions; pin a public key and ship a spare pin

rubric: Pinning a single leaf with no spare makes rotation an outage for installed apps; key pinning plus a backup avoids it.
Pinning does protect against rogue CAs, and stores allow it.

items.prompt: In a 5% staged rollout, overall crash-free sessions are 99.6%, but on Android 9 devices they fall to 93%, traced to one new native call. Criteria: protect users, keep learning. Best action?

options.label: Pull the update from every user at once, because any regression requires a complete revert of the release
Halt expansion, fix or gate the call for that OS version, and resume once that cohort recovers
Continue the rollout, since overall crash-free sessions are above target and the affected cohort is small
Wait until 50% rollout to gather statistically meaningful data on the Android 9 cohort before acting

rubric: A cohort-specific regression with a known cause justifies pausing and fixing, while the rollout continues to teach you.
Aggregate metrics hide cohort failures; waiting grows the harm.

items.prompt: Five web developers must ship a field-inspection app on both platforms in 4 months. It needs offline forms, camera capture and one image-analysis step that must run at native speed. Which is the best trade-off?

options.label: Use a cross-platform framework for UI and forms, with the analysis step in a native module behind a thin bridge
Wrap the existing website in a web view, since it maximises reuse and browser caching can cover offline forms
Use a cross-platform framework only, running the analysis in its default language runtime for a single codebase
Build two fully native apps, because one native-speed requirement means every screen should be native

rubric: Cross-platform for most screens meets the team and schedule limits, and a native module isolates the one performance need.
Fully native ignores the team and timeline; pure runtime code misses the speed requirement.

items.prompt: Evaluate approaches to local database upgrades for an app whose users often skip several releases and hold unsynced data. Which judgments are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Migrations should run in sequence so a user on any old version reaches the current schema
Upgrade tests should start from the oldest supported schema with realistic data, not only fresh installs
A failed migration should leave the database consistent, for example by running inside a transaction
Editing an already-released migration is safe as long as fresh installs pass their tests
Dropping and recreating tables is acceptable because the server can always resend the data

rubric: Sequential, tested, atomic migrations protect users who skip versions.
Drop-and-recreate destroys unsynced data, and editing shipped migrations breaks devices already migrated.

items.prompt: An Android feed screen janks on low-end phones. Profiling shows 4000x3000 JPEGs fully decoded on the main thread to fill 100dp thumbnails, with memory spikes causing occasional out-of-memory kills. Criteria: fix the root cause, keep thumbnails sharp, add little complexity. Which option is best?

options.label: Request server-resized thumbnails and decode downsampled bitmaps off the main thread via an image loader with a cache
Enable the large-heap flag and keep decoding on the main thread, so memory limits stop triggering process kills
Cut the page size to five items so fewer full-size images are decoded at the same time while scrolling
Convert thumbnails to grayscale after decoding, which lowers memory use while keeping them recognisable

rubric: The cause is oversized decoding on the main thread; downsampling off-thread with caching fixes both jank and memory.
Large heap, smaller pages and grayscale treat symptoms and leave the full-size decode in place.

items.prompt: Design the write path for an expense app on flaky networks. Constraints: no entries lost after the app is killed, no duplicates when a request succeeds but its response is lost, per-user order preserved. Which design meets all three?

options.label: Persist an outbox, retry all entries in parallel for speed, and dedupe on the device timestamp of each entry
Retry each request in an in-memory loop, and have the server reject entries with identical amounts and dates
Persist an outbox but let the server assign each ID on receipt, and retry until a response arrives for each entry
Persist each mutation in a local outbox with a client-generated ID, replay in order, and dedupe by ID on the server

rubric: Durable outbox, client IDs for idempotency and ordered replay satisfy all constraints.
Server-assigned IDs cannot dedupe a lost response; parallel retries break order; memory-only retries lose entries.

items.prompt: Design links for marketing emails. They must open a product screen if the app is installed, open the website if not, and not be interceptable by another app claiming the same scheme. Which design meets all three?

options.label: Verified HTTPS links (Universal Links / App Links) tied to the domain, with web pages as fallback without the app
HTTPS links that always open the website, which then shows an Open in App button using a custom scheme
A custom scheme with an unusual name, plus a server-side referrer check to block other apps from claiming it
A custom URI scheme such as shop://product/42, with a web redirect if the scheme fails to open

rubric: Domain-verified HTTPS links open the app when present, fall back to the web, and cannot be claimed by other apps.
Custom schemes are unverified and can be hijacked; referrer checks cannot stop OS-level claims.

items.prompt: Design a checkout flow where the user may switch to a banking app mid-checkout and the OS may kill your process. Constraints: return to the same step with entered data, and never persist card data. Which design meets both?

options.label: Set a keep-awake flag for the whole checkout session so the OS will not reclaim the process while the user is in the banking app
Hold the whole checkout in an in-memory singleton shared by all screens, since it survives screen changes and background transitions
Persist every field including the card number, encrypted with a key bundled inside the app, and restore them all on return
Save the step and non-sensitive fields in saved state by route, and re-prompt card entry via a tokenised input

rubric: Serializable non-sensitive state survives process death, and card data is re-requested instead of stored.
Singletons die with the process, bundled keys are extractable, and keep-awake does not prevent process death.

items.prompt: Design how to ship a breaking API change when old app versions stay installed for months and store review can't be rushed. Constraints: old versions work until a cut-off, users are then guided to update, and the cut-off can be set without a new release. Which design meets all?

options.label: Version the API, keep old versions served, and have the app check a server-set minimum version at launch to prompt updates
Make new fields optional and let the server infer each client's capabilities from the device model string sent in request headers
Deploy the breaking change at once and rely on automatic store updates to move nearly every user to the new version within a day
Hardcode the cut-off date into the next release to trigger the update prompt, then ship the API change on that date for all users

rubric: Versioned endpoints plus a server-controlled minimum version meet every constraint.
Auto-updates are unreliable, hardcoded dates need a release, and device model is not a capability signal.

items.prompt: Design uploads of 500 MB videos from phones. Constraints: uploads continue after the user leaves the app, survive flaky connections without restarting from zero, and respect iOS and Android background limits. Which design meets all?

options.label: Chunked upload driven by a JavaScript or Dart timer in the background, resuming from the last saved chunk whenever the timer fires
A single multipart POST from a foreground service or background task that keeps the app awake until the upload ends, with automatic retry on failure
Compress the video to 50 MB in the foreground first, then send it in one request and retry from the start on any network failure
Chunked resumable upload via OS-managed background transfers (URLSession background / WorkManager), recording acknowledged chunks

rubric: OS-managed background transfers with resumable chunks satisfy survival, resumption and platform limits.
Timers and long-held tasks are suspended or killed, and single-request uploads restart from zero.

items.prompt: Design a session scheme: users stay signed in for weeks, a stolen device's access can be revoked, and no secrets ship in the app binary. Which elements must the design include? Select all that apply.

options.label: Short-lived access tokens refreshed using a refresh token
Per-device refresh tokens that the server can revoke individually
A shared API secret obfuscated inside the binary to sign each request
The refresh token kept in Keychain or Keystore, not plain preferences
A one-year access token in local preferences to avoid refresh logic

rubric: Short-lived access tokens, secure storage and server-side per-device revocation meet all three constraints.
Obfuscated secrets are extractable, and a one-year token cannot be revoked quickly.

items.prompt: A team proposes third-party sign-in by loading the provider's login page in an in-app WebView and reading the redirect URL for the auth code. A client secret is embedded in the app. Reviewers say the design is missing a key element for security. Which change addresses it?

options.label: Obfuscate the client secret with string encryption and have the WebView check that the redirect host matches the registered callback before accepting the code
Use a system browser session (ASWebAuthenticationSession / Custom Tabs) with the code flow and PKCE, not a secret
Keep the WebView but move the client secret into the keychain or keystore, so the app can still read it to exchange the code and the user stays in-app
Switch to the implicit flow so no secret is needed and tokens arrive directly in the redirect URL, avoiding a code exchange step on the device

rubric: System browser sessions keep credentials out of the app, and PKCE replaces an extractable secret for public clients.
Obfuscation is reversible, implicit flow is discouraged, and auto-filling credentials worsens exposure.
